tag: The Pink City of palaces, forts and bazaars
ab: Jaipur was planned in 1727 by Maharaja Jai Singh II, an astronomer-king, and painted pink to welcome a prince in 1876. Hilltop forts guard a walled city of bazaars and havelis.
ppl: Jaipur's old city is organised by craft: one bazaar for bangles, another for silver, a lane of block-printers in Sanganer and blue-pottery makers nearby. Rajput families still celebrate Teej and Gangaur with women in leheriya saris carrying idols through the streets, and every home welcomes guests with 'padharo mhare des'.

places.d: A honey-coloured fort-palace above Maota Lake, with a Hall of Mirrors that glitters in candlelight.
A five-storey honeycomb of 953 windows built so royal women could watch street life unseen.
places.t: The best photo is from the cafés across the road.

places.d: Still home to the royal family, with the Peacock Gate and giant silver urns.
Giant stone astronomical instruments, including a sundial accurate to two seconds.
The ridge-top fort above the city, with the best view over the pink city; its Padao café stays open for sunset.
A criss-cross stepwell near Amber, perfectly symmetrical and quieter than the forts.
A military fort holding Jaivana, once the world's largest cannon on wheels.
An Indo-Saracenic museum with an Egyptian mummy, lit up beautifully at night.
Gemstones, mojari shoes, bandhani and block-printed quilts in the arcades of the pink city.
Temples and natural spring pools in a rocky gorge, home to troops of monkeys.
A recreated Rajasthani village with folk dance, puppets and a huge thali.
A palace that seems to float in the middle of Man Sagar lake.

tag: The City of Lakes, India's most romantic
ab: Udaipur, capital of the Mewar kings, rises from the shores of Lake Pichola with white palaces, ghats and island hotels set against the Aravalli hills.
ppl: Mewar's Rajputs take pride in never having bowed to the Mughals. In the old city, miniature painters work with squirrel-hair brushes, women in odhnis gather at the ghats each morning, and evenings at Bagore ki Haveli bring Ghoomar and Bhavai dances, a woman balancing a tower of pots on her head.
go: Maharana Pratap Airport 22 km; Udaipur City station

places.d: A wedding cake of balconies and courtyards above Lake Pichola, with mirror rooms and peacock mosaics.
Cruise past the Lake Palace to Jag Mandir island as the palaces glow at sunset.
A carved 1651 Vishnu temple at the heart of the old city, busy with morning aarti.

places.n: Dharohar dance at Bagore ki Haveli
places.d: An hour of Rajasthani folk dance and puppets in an 18th-century haveli courtyard.
A hilltop palace built to watch monsoon clouds; the best sunset over the lakes.
The classic view of the City Palace across the water, beautiful at night.
A garden of fountains and marble elephants built for the queen's companions.
A wide lake with a promenade where locals gather for chai and corn in the evening.
A fort with the second-longest wall in the world, 36 km around, on a ridge 85 km away.
A crafts village of traditional huts from four states, with potters and musicians.

tag: The Blue City under a mighty fort
ab: Jodhpur's old city is a maze of blue houses below Mehrangarh, one of India's greatest forts, on the edge of the Thar desert.
ppl: Brahmin families first painted their homes blue, and the colour spread because it keeps houses cool. Old Jodhpur life spills onto rooftops and stepwells; Marwari traders, Bishnoi villagers who protect every tree and blackbuck, and turbaned musicians all meet at the clock-tower market.

places.d: A fort that grows out of a 125 m cliff, with palaces of carved sandstone and a superb museum.
A translucent white-marble memorial with lake views of the fort.
Wander indigo lanes, tiny temples and doorsteps where families sit out in the afternoon.
A restored 18th-century stepwell of rose sandstone in the old city.
One of the world's largest private homes, part palace hotel, part museum of Art Deco treasures.
Spices, bangles and textiles around the clock tower; try a makhaniya lassi.
Trails through restored native desert plants on volcanic rock beneath the fort walls.
Red sandstone cenotaphs of Marwar's rulers in an old capital's gardens.

tag: The Golden City and the dunes of the Thar
ab: Jaisalmer's sandstone fort rises like a sandcastle from the Thar desert, a living fort where a quarter of the town still lives. The Sam dunes are 40 km west.
ppl: Inside the fort, families have lived for 850 years. Manganiyar and Langa musicians, hereditary singers to their patrons, sing desert ballads with kamaicha and khartal. Out in the dunes, Rabari herders in white with big gold earrings tend camels, and women build round mud huts decorated with mirror-work.

places.d: A living fort of golden stone with Jain temples, havelis and homes inside its walls.
Five merchant mansions with stone carved as finely as lace.
The old water tank lined with shrines and chhatris, golden at sunrise.
Camel rides over rolling dunes at sunset, then folk music under the stars.
A Paliwal Brahmin village deserted overnight 200 years ago, its roofless houses still standing.
Royal chhatris on a hill with wind turbines behind; magical at sunset.
A ruined fort above another abandoned Paliwal village, with peacocks and desert silence.
A haveli with a peacock-shaped roof and 38 balconies.

tag: A holy lake, a Brahma temple and the great camel fair
ab: Pushkar is a small holy town around a sacred lake with 52 ghats, home to one of the world's few Brahma temples. Each November the camel fair brings tens of thousands of herders.
ppl: Pushkar is vegetarian and alcohol-free. Pujaris at the ghats offer 'Pushkar passport' blessings, Rebari herders arrive for the fair with camels decorated in tassels and anklets, and in the lanes you'll hear bhajans from the 500 temples all day.
go: Ajmer Junction 15 km; Jaipur airport 150 km

places.d: A rare temple to Lord Brahma, the creator, with a red spire and marble steps.
Pilgrims bathe and float lamps on 52 ghats; the sunset aarti is the best time.
A hilltop temple to Brahma's wife, reached by steps or ropeway, with a view of the town and desert.
Silver jewellery, rose products and cotton clothes along the narrow main street.
Thousands of camels and herders, moustache contests and folk performers for a week in November.

tag: Rajasthan's only hill station and the finest marble temples
ab: Mount Abu is a cool green plateau in the Aravallis with Nakki Lake at its centre and the Dilwara Jain temples, whose marble carving is among the finest in the world.
ppl: Garasia tribal families live in the forests around Abu and come to town for markets and fairs. Jain pilgrims arrive in white, and Gujarati families escape the summer heat here, so the evening lakeside is busy with snacks, boating and couples.

places.d: 11th–13th century temples where marble is carved so thin it looks transparent.
A lake ringed by hills and odd rocks like Toad Rock, with boating.
The highest point of the Aravallis (1,722 m) with a small Dattatreya temple.
Crowds gather to watch the sun sink into the plains.
A ruined fort with an old Shiva temple and a toe print of the god.
A forested reservoir for birds, crocodiles and the occasional sloth bear.

tag: Tigers among the ruins of a thousand-year-old fort
ab: Ranthambore is the best-known tiger reserve in India, a dry forest of lakes, banyan trees and ruined pavilions below a hilltop fort.
ppl: Meena and Mogya villagers live around the park, and many families once depended on its forests; today their sons drive the safari Gypsies and their mothers run the Dastkar crafts cooperative. Every Wednesday, the Ganesh temple inside the fort receives thousands of wedding invitation cards by post.
fest: Ganesh Chaturthi fair at the fort

places.d: Jeep or canter safaris through lakes and ruins where tigers walk in daylight.
places.t: Book Gypsy permits online as soon as dates open.

places.d: A UNESCO hill fort with step wells, temples and views over the jungle.
A three-eyed Ganesh inside the fort, sent letters and wedding cards from across India.
Village women's patchwork, block prints and toys sold at fair prices.
A seasonal lake full of flamingos, storks and cranes in winter.

tag: India's largest fort and its legends of valour
ab: Chittorgarh Fort covers 700 acres on a 180 m hill, with towers of victory, palaces and water tanks. Its sieges and the story of Rani Padmini are central to Rajput history.
ppl: For Rajputs, Chittor is the symbol of honour; folk singers still sing of Rana Kumbha, Padmini and the saint-poet Meera Bai, who worshipped Krishna here. Local guides are often the grandsons of guides.

places.d: Seven gates, palaces, temples and tanks spread across a vast hilltop.
A nine-storey tower of victory covered in carved gods, built in 1448.
A water palace linked to the legend of Rani Padmini.
The fort's history told in the evening at Rana Kumbha's palace.

tag: A white salt desert under the full moon
ab: The Great Rann of Kutch is a vast white salt marsh that dries in winter into a glittering plain. Bhuj is the base, with crafts villages scattered across the desert.
ppl: Kutch is India's craft heartland: Rabari women embroider mirror-work, Ahir and Meghwal families paint and weave, and in Nirona one Khatri family keeps alive rogan art, painting cloth with castor-oil paint using a metal stick. Round bhunga huts with mud-and-mirror walls stay cool in summer and survive earthquakes.

places.d: A white salt desert to the horizon; at full moon it glows silver.
places.t: Get the BSF permit online or at Bhirandiyara.

places.d: The highest point in Kutch, looking over the Rann toward Pakistan.
Watch rogan painting, bell-making and lacquer work in family homes.
Mud-and-mirror bhunga huts, embroidery and the famous mawa sweet of Bhirandiyara.
Bhuj's mirror palace and an Italian-Gothic palace with a clock tower view.
A quiet beach and a palace where shipbuilders still make wooden dhows by hand.
A ghost port town inside 18th-century walls at India's western edge.

tag: India's first World Heritage City and Gandhi's ashram
ab: Ahmedabad's walled city of pols, carved wooden homes in gated lanes, made it India's first UNESCO World Heritage City. Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram and great stepwells are nearby.
ppl: Families in the old pols share courtyards, wells and bird feeders called chabutaras, and know every neighbour's business. On Uttarayan in January, the whole city is on its rooftops flying kites from dawn, and during Navratri everyone dances garba until 2 AM.
go: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport; Ahmedabad Junction

places.d: Gandhi's riverside home from 1917 to 1930, where the Salt March began.
A morning walk through gated pols of carved havelis, temples and bird feeders.
A five-storey stepwell of 1499 with carved pillars and cool, filtered light.
Famous for its stone lattice windows carved as a tree of life.
A jewellery square by day that becomes a giant street-food court at night.
A UNESCO stepwell with 500 sculptures, the one on the ₹100 note.
A 1026 temple aligned so the equinox sun lights up its sanctum, beside a stepped tank.
A lakefront with a toy train, zoo and evening food stalls.

tag: The last home of the Asiatic lion
ab: Gir is the only place in the world where Asiatic lions live in the wild, now over 600 of them, in dry teak forest. The park closes for the monsoon from mid-June to mid-October.
ppl: The Maldhari herders live inside the forest in nesses of mud huts with their buffaloes, sharing the land with lions for centuries. Siddi families, descended from East Africans who came centuries ago, perform the energetic Dhamal dance in villages like Jambur.

places.d: Jeep safaris through teak and grassland for lions, leopards and spotted deer.
places.t: Permits open on the official portal; book early for winter weekends.

places.d: A fenced zone inside Gir where lion sightings are almost certain; good with kids.
A reservoir in the forest with marsh crocodiles basking on its banks.
Afro-Gujarati Siddi musicians perform the trance-like Dhamal with drums and shells.

tag: Krishna's kingdom by the Arabian Sea
ab: Dwarka is one of the Char Dham, believed to be Krishna's capital. The Dwarkadhish temple rises over the Gomti river mouth, and Bet Dwarka island is now reached by India's longest cable-stayed bridge.
ppl: The temple's flag is changed five times a day and families book years ahead to sponsor one. Fishing families of the Kharwa community launch boats from Okha, and on Janmashtami the whole town dances raas through the night.
go: Dwarka railway station; Jamnagar airport 130 km

places.d: A five-storey temple on 72 pillars whose huge flag flies over the sea.
An island temple where Krishna lived, now reached by a 2.3 km cable-stayed bridge.
One of the twelve Jyotirlingas, with a giant seated Shiva statue outside.
A Blue Flag beach with clear water, snorkelling and scuba in season.
A richly carved 12th-century temple to Krishna's wife, standing alone outside town.
Steps down to where the Gomti meets the sea, beneath the temple.

tag: The first Jyotirlinga by the sea, and Portuguese Diu
ab: Somnath temple stands on the shore where nothing lies between it and Antarctica. Diu, 90 km away, is a former Portuguese island of forts, churches and quiet beaches.
ppl: Somnath has been destroyed and rebuilt many times, and pilgrims see it as a symbol of resilience. In Diu, Portuguese-speaking grandparents, fishing families and Gujarati traders share whitewashed lanes, and the evening tide-watch on the fort walls is a daily ritual.
go: Veraval railway station 7 km; Diu airport

places.d: The first of the twelve Jyotirlingas, rebuilt in 1951 on the edge of the Arabian Sea.
The temple's story told against its own walls with the sea behind.
Where three rivers meet the sea; pilgrims bathe before darshan.
A 1535 Portuguese sea fort with cannons, a lighthouse and a prison island offshore.
A web of quarried caves with sunlight falling through holes in the roof.
A horseshoe beach lined with hoka palms found nowhere else in India.
A Baroque church of 1610 with a carved wooden altar.

tag: The world's tallest statue on the Narmada
ab: The 182 m Statue of Unity of Sardar Patel stands on an island facing the Sardar Sarovar Dam, with gardens, a jungle safari and river cruises around it.
ppl: Tadvi and Bhil Adivasi villages surround Kevadia, and many young people from these villages now work as guides and drivers. Look for their warli-style wall paintings and bamboo crafts at the haat.
go: Ekta Nagar railway station; Vadodara airport 90 km

places.d: Lifts take you 153 m up inside the statue to look out over the dam and the Satpura hills.
A huge concrete dam on the Narmada, spectacular when its gates open in the monsoon.
Projection on the statue telling Sardar Patel's story.
A large zoological park of Indian and world animals, good with children.
A boat ride on the reservoir past the statue and forested hills.

tag: The maximum city of sea faces, film stars and vada pav
ab: Mumbai is India's busiest, richest city, built on seven islands: Gothic railway stations and Art Deco seafronts, Bollywood, ancient cave temples and a street food culture that never stops.
ppl: Mumbai runs on the local train and the dabbawalas, who deliver 200,000 home-cooked lunches a day with a colour-code system. Koli fisherfolk, the city's first people, still live in Worli and Versova villages. Ganeshotsav turns the whole city into a festival, and everybody, rich or poor, eats vada pav.
go: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport; CSMT and Mumbai Central stations

places.d: A basalt arch on the waterfront built for King George V, opposite the Taj Palace hotel.
An hour's ferry ride to a rock-cut cave temple with the giant three-headed Shiva.
A Victorian Gothic railway station, still India's busiest, lit up at night.
The 'Queen's Necklace' seafront where all of Mumbai comes to watch the sun go down.
Indian sculpture, miniatures and Tibetan art in a domed Indo-Saracenic building.
A white shrine on an islet reached by a causeway that floods at high tide.
The world's biggest open-air laundry, where washermen have beaten clothes clean for 130 years.
An ancient temple tank hidden among the mansions of Malabar Hill.
Galleries, Art Deco cafés and the David Sassoon library in the old fort area.
Pav bhaji, bhel and gola on the sand as the sun sets.
A Portuguese fort ruin and sea walk past film stars' homes, with the Sea Link view.
109 Buddhist caves inside a forest national park, in the middle of the city.
Mumbai's favourite Ganesh temple, busy with film stars and commuters alike.

tag: Monsoon waterfalls, forts and chikki in the Sahyadris
ab: Lonavala sits on the Sahyadri crest between Mumbai and Pune; in the monsoon its cliffs run with waterfalls, and ancient Buddhist caves and Maratha forts crown the hills.
ppl: The Sahyadri forts are a pilgrimage for Maharashtrians, who trek them in groups singing praises of Shivaji Maharaj. Village families around Pawna run lakeside camps, and Lonavala's chikki makers, many of them Gujarati families, have made peanut-jaggery sweets for a century.
go: Lonavala station on the Mumbai–Pune line

places.d: A 2,000-year-old Buddhist prayer hall with a wooden ribbed ceiling, the largest of its kind.
22 rock-cut caves with early stupas and a waterfall beside them in the monsoon.
An easy trek to a Maratha fort with the scorpion-tail 'Vinchu Kata' ridge.
A 650 m cliff edge above the Konkan, full of waterfalls in the rains.
Water pours over the dam steps in the monsoon and families sit right in it.
Lakeside tents, barbecue and stargazing with Tung and Tikona forts behind.

tag: Asia's only car-free hill station, with red earth paths
ab: Matheran bans all vehicles: you arrive by toy train or on foot and explore red-earth forest paths to dozens of cliff-edge viewpoints over the Western Ghats.
ppl: Without cars, Matheran moves on horses, hand-pulled rickshaws and porters, many from the Dhangar shepherd and Katkari tribal communities. Families run old Parsi and Bohra bungalows as guesthouses, and the town falls quiet after dark.
go: Neral station, then toy train or taxi to Dasturi

places.d: A 1907 narrow-gauge train climbing 21 km of hairpins through forest.
A 360° view of the ghats; sunrise here is the best in town.
A cliff with waterfalls and the ruins of Prabal fort across the valley.
The town's water source, ringed by forest and a small temple.
A lone tree on a jutting hill, reached by a forest trail.
Shout into the valley and hear it answer back.

tag: Strawberry farms, misty points and a Shivaji fort
ab: Mahabaleshwar is a plateau of forest and viewpoints where five rivers rise; strawberry farms fill the slopes in winter, and Shivaji's Pratapgad fort is nearby.
ppl: Farmers here grow most of India's strawberries, and from December families sell them fresh with cream at roadside stalls. In Old Mahabaleshwar, the Krishna river's source is a temple where water flows from a cow's mouth, and pilgrims come from all over Maharashtra.

places.d: The 'queen of points', a cliff dropping into the Savitri valley.
Boating and horse rides around a lake lined with snack stalls.
Where Shivaji defeated Afzal Khan in 1659; walls with views to the Konkan.
Pick strawberries in the fields and eat them with fresh cream.
A flat volcanic plateau, one of Asia's largest, with caves and sunset views.
The source of the Krishna river, flowing from a carved cow's mouth.
A 180 m waterfall into the Venna valley, at its best after the monsoon.

tag: Two thousand years of art carved into rock
ab: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) is the base for Ellora's 34 Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, including the Kailasa temple carved from a single rock, and Ajanta's painted Buddhist caves.
ppl: Weavers in the old city still make Himroo shawls and Paithani silk on wooden looms, a craft from the Nizams' time. Villagers near Ajanta remember the British officer who stumbled on the caves while hunting a tiger in 1819.

places.d: 34 caves including Kailasa, a whole temple cut downward from one mountain of basalt.
Buddhist caves in a horseshoe gorge with paintings from the 2nd century BC.
places.t: Closed on Mondays; it's a 2.5-hour drive each way.

places.d: The 'Taj of the Deccan', built by Aurangzeb's son for his mother.
A hill fort with a dark spiral tunnel and a moat that once held crocodiles.
The twelfth Jyotirlinga, a red-stone temple right beside Ellora.
Visit a weaving workshop near Panchakki to see Himroo shawls made on old looms.

tag: Sai Baba's town, open to every faith
ab: Shirdi grew around the samadhi of Sai Baba, a saint revered by Hindus and Muslims alike. Shani Shingnapur, the village with no doors, is 70 km away.
ppl: Sai devotees chant 'Sabka Malik Ek' (one God for all) and the Sansthan feeds tens of thousands every day. In Shani Shingnapur, families trust the deity so completely that houses, shops and even the bank have no locks on their doors.

places.d: The marble shrine over Sai Baba's tomb; the kakad aarti at dawn is moving.
The mosque where Baba lived, with the sacred fire (dhuni) he lit still burning.
The places where Baba slept on alternate nights and first appeared as a young man.
An open-air Shani shrine and a village where homes have no doors.
A recreation of Shirdi as it was in Baba's time.

tag: Beaches, forts, flea markets and Goa's party coast
ab: North Goa runs from Candolim to Arambol: busy beaches and nightlife, Portuguese forts on red cliffs, the World Heritage churches of Old Goa and Panaji's Latin quarter.
ppl: Goan life is susegad: unhurried. Catholic families with Portuguese surnames live in colourful houses with balcões (porch seats), and the bakery boy still cycles round at dawn honking a horn. Feni is distilled from cashew in village stills, and fishermen's wooden canoes line every beach at dawn.

places.d: A 1612 Portuguese fort and lighthouse at the mouth of the Mandovi.
Red laterite walls above Vagator beach, with a sweeping sunset view.

places.n: Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa
places.d: The baroque church holding St Francis Xavier's body, with Sé Cathedral across the lawn.
Panaji's Latin quarter of yellow, blue and green Portuguese houses and tiny bakeries.
Every Wednesday since the 1960s: Tibetan, Kashmiri and Goan stalls on a beach headland.
Saturday nights only: food stalls, live music and crafts under fairy lights.
Goa's busiest beaches: water sports by day, beach shacks and clubs by night.
A laid-back beach with a freshwater lake behind it and drum circles at sunset.
A free ferry to a quiet island of paddy fields, churches and old Goan homes.
A four-tiered 310 m waterfall like spilled milk, reached by jeep through the forest.
Goa's most famous street of clubs and bars.

tag: Quiet palm-fringed bays and old Portuguese mansions
ab: South Goa is calmer: crescent beaches like Palolem and Agonda, hidden coves, a cliff fort and grand Portuguese-era mansions in villages like Chandor.
ppl: In Chandor and Loutolim, old Goan families still live in 300-year-old mansions full of Chinese porcelain and chandeliers, and some open their doors to visitors. Turtle-protecting fishermen at Galgibaga guard Olive Ridley nests on the beach each winter.

places.d: A perfect crescent of sand and palms, with kayaking to Butterfly Beach.
A clifftop fort with a little church and a path down to a secret beach.
A hidden cove reached only by boat or forest trail, where dolphins often swim.
A long, peaceful beach where turtles nest and huts stand on stilts.
A lagoon meets the sea between forested hills, one of Goa's prettiest spots.
A 17th-century mansion with a ballroom, still lived in by the same family.
An empty beach of casuarinas where Olive Ridley turtles nest in winter.
A tour of pepper, cardamom and nutmeg gardens ending with a Goan lunch on banana leaves.
A long white beach where local families come in the evening.
